new_statements.quote: Sambe was transcribed with three level tones and a rising and falling tone. [...] Vowels without tones marked are therefore mid. Initial nasals, such as m- may or may not be tone-bearing. The tone, which is always low, is marked where it was heard. There was some variation in tone between the two sessions, so the tones cannot be considered wholly reliable.
new_statements.citation: Blench, Roger. 2015. Final Records of the Sambe Language of Central Nigeria: Phonology, Noun Morphology, and Wordlist. Language Documentation & Conservation 9: 192–228. http://hdl.handle.net/10125/24641
new_statements.locator: §3.3 Tones, p. 199 (PDF p. 8); caveat at §3 Phonology, p. 194
new_statements.rule_in_words: Sambe is described as a tone language with three level tones (high, mid, low) plus rising and falling contours; the source says nothing at all about word stress or accent, so no stress placement rule can be extracted.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. The author warns (p. 194) that 'the informants' tone was somewhat unstable and no conclusions should be drawn from the tone, which was marked as heard'; data were written by ear without a recorder from two to six very aged speakers in 2001 and 2005.
new_statements.domain_note: Wordlist citation forms only (isolated lexical items); no phrase-level or intonational description.
new_statements.identity_note: The source describes Sambe [xab] = samb1307 exactly: the single village of Sambe (Kaduna State, near Agameti on the Fadan Karshe–Wamba road), closest relative Hasha, Alumic subgroup of Plateau. No dialects; Sambe had earlier been misfiled as a dialect of Ninzo (ninz1244) in Ethnologue, but Blench states it is not a Ninzo dialect. Language presumed extinct after 2005 (two speakers aged ~90 and ~85).
